config.title: Write a custom filter polyfill

intro.title: Write a custom filter polyfill
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a custom version of the JavaScript `filter` method, called `myFilter`, from scratch. You will learn how to implement a function that iterates over an array and returns a new array containing only the elements that pass a test defined by a callback function. The core programming concept used is array iteration and conditional logic, applying a function to each element. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, arrays, loops, and callbacks. This exercise will deepen your understanding of how higher-order array methods work internally. By the end, you will have a working polyfill that mimics the native `filter` method's behavior.
intro.usecase: The filter method is a core tool for developers building interactive data-driven interfaces. In real-world applications, you use it to dynamically display search results in an e-commerce product list, filter tasks by status in a project management dashboard, or show only unread messages in an email client. Understanding how to build your own filter polyfill ensures your applications remain functional across different browser environments, a common requirement for professional web development.

objectives: Implement a function that accepts an array and a callback as arguments.
Construct a new array to store filtered elements based on callback logic.
Apply the callback to each element, using its value, index, and original array.
Manipulate the new array by conditionally pushing elements when the callback returns true.
Initialize and return the new array containing only the filtered items.
Integrate the custom filter function into a script and test it with sample data.
Control the iteration process to handle edge cases like empty arrays or sparse arrays.

steps.title: Create a test array and define the filter polyfill function
steps.instruction: Create a test array of numbers and define an empty customFilter function that accepts a callback parameter.
steps.hint: Start by declaring an array with some numbers, then define a function named customFilter that takes a callback parameter.
steps.seedCode: // Create a test array of numbers and define an empty customFilter function that accepts a callback
steps.expectedOutcome: You should have an array variable and a function definition with the correct name and parameter.
successCriteria: An array of numbers is declared and a function named customFilter is defined with a callback parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have both the array and the function definition with a callback parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: create an array of numbers and define a function named customFilter that accepts a callback.

steps.title: Initialize an empty results array inside the function
steps.instruction: Inside the customFilter function, create an empty array to store the filtered results.
steps.hint: Declare a variable inside the function and assign it an empty array [].
steps.expectedOutcome: The customFilter function will have a variable declared to hold the filtered items.
successCriteria: An empty array variable is declared inside the customFilter function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up storage for the filtered results.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you declare an empty array variable inside the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The step requires creating an empty array inside the customFilter function.

steps.title: Add a for loop to iterate through the array
steps.instruction: Inside the customFilter function, add a traditional for loop that iterates through each element of the numbers array using an index variable.
steps.hint: Use a for loop with an index variable (like i) that starts at 0 and continues while i is less than the array length.
steps.expectedOutcome: The customFilter function will contain a for loop that can iterate through each element of the numbers array.
successCriteria: A for loop is added inside the customFilter function that iterates through the numbers array using an index variable.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your for loop correctly iterates through the entire numbers array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The for loop structure isn't quite right. Remember to use the correct syntax: for (let i = 0; i < numbers.length; i++)

steps.title: Call the callback function with current element
steps.instruction: Inside the for loop, call the callback function with the current array element as its argument.
steps.hint: Use the callback parameter name from the function signature and pass the current element (e.g., callback(currentElement)).
steps.expectedOutcome: The callback function is invoked for each element in the array during iteration.
successCriteria: The callback function is called inside the loop with the current element as its argument.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're calling the callback function with the current element as an argument.
steps.feedbackWrong: The callback function needs to be called inside the loop with the current element as its argument. Try using callback(this[i]) or callback(currentElement).

steps.title: Check the callback's return value
steps.instruction: Inside the for loop, store the callback's return value in a variable and add an if statement to check if it's truthy.
steps.hint: Call the callback with the current element (this[i]) and store the result. Then use an if statement to check if that result is truthy.
steps.expectedOutcome: The callback's return value is stored and checked for truthiness, preparing to push matching elements to the results array.
successCriteria: The callback is called with this[i] and its return value is stored in a variable. An if statement checks if that value is truthy.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're calling the callback with this[i] and storing the result, then checking it with an if statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on this step: store the callback's return value when called with the current element, then check if it's truthy with an if statement.

steps.title: Push matching elements to results array
steps.instruction: Inside the if statement, push the current element (this[i]) to the results array when the callback returns truthy.
steps.hint: Use the push method on the results array with the current element as the argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: The customFilter function now collects matching elements in the results array when the callback returns true.
successCriteria: The if statement includes a push call to add this[i] to the results array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're pushing the current element (this[i]) to the results array inside the if block.
steps.feedbackWrong: The push operation is missing or incorrect. Inside the if statement, use results.push(this[i]) to add the element.

steps.title: Return the results array
steps.instruction: After the for loop, add a return statement to return the results array from the customFilter function.
steps.hint: Use the 'return' keyword followed by the array variable name.
steps.expectedOutcome: The customFilter function now returns the filtered results array.
successCriteria: The customFilter function includes a return statement that returns the results array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're returning the 'results' array variable.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function needs to return the results array. Add 'return results;' after the loop.

steps.title: Test the polyfill with a simple callback
steps.instruction: Call the customFilter function on the numbers array with a callback that filters numbers greater than 2, and log the result to the console.
steps.hint: Use numbers.customFilter(callback) where the callback returns true when the element is greater than 2.
steps.expectedOutcome: The console should log [3, 4, 5] when the polyfill is called with the correct callback.
successCriteria: customFilter is called on numbers with a callback that checks if each element is greater than 2, and the result is logged.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling customFilter on the numbers array and logging the result.
steps.feedbackWrong: The test didn't produce the expected output. Check that you're calling the function correctly and the callback returns true for numbers > 2.

steps.title: Add index parameter to callback
steps.instruction: Modify the callback call inside your for loop to pass both the current element and the current index as arguments.
steps.hint: Update the line where you call callback(this[i]) to include i as the second argument.
steps.expectedOutcome: The callback function will receive both the element and its index when called during iteration.
successCriteria: The callback is called with two arguments: this[i] and i.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're passing both arguments: the current element (this[i]) and the current index (i).
steps.feedbackWrong: The callback should receive two arguments: the current element and its index. Try updating the callback call to include both.

steps.title: Test with index-based filtering
steps.instruction: Test your customFilter polyfill by calling it on the numbers array with a callback that uses the index parameter to filter elements at even positions (where index % 2 === 0).
steps.hint: Use the callback function's second parameter (index) to check if the position is even, then return true for those elements.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: filtering even-indexed elements
const filtered = numbers.filter((num, idx) => idx % 2 === 0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The polyfill should correctly filter elements based on their index position, returning [1, 3, 5] when filtering for even indices.
successCriteria: The customFilter function is called with a callback that uses the index parameter to filter elements at even positions, and the result is logged or stored.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your callback uses the index parameter (second argument) to check if the position is even (index % 2 === 0).
steps.feedbackWrong: The test doesn't use index-based filtering. Remember to pass both element and index to the callback, then check if index % 2 === 0.
